01 / Building on what is already working

We don't start from zero. We build on what Saudi Arabia has already started.

Saudi agencies are already planting, seeding clouds and protecting land at national scale. The hard part now is keeping it alive, proving the results and reaching places people can't. That is exactly where autonomous aircraft help.

02 / Continuation of the national program

One factory. One fleet. Many national missions.

This climate program is not a separate business. It runs on the same Saudi industrial base proposed in Part I, the National Autonomous Systems Program.

  1. Built in the KingdomA Saudi aerospace campus of about 55,000 m² with 106 technical jobs, where the aircraft are built, converted and maintained.
  2. One shared fleetEGX-10, EGX-200 and converted helicopters, with the same software, ground control and training.
  3. Climate missionsTrees, water, mangroves, clouds, dust, highlands, wildlife and remote logistics.
  4. Saudi resultsSaudi-owned data and verified results, reported to Saudi agencies.
  • Daily civil work for the factoryClimate missions keep Saudi operators and technicians flying and maintaining aircraft every day, not only for security tasks.
  • One investment, two returnsPart I already pays for the aircraft, training and flight-test center. Climate missions put that same fleet to more use. No second factory is needed.
  • Saudi green-tech jobsNew careers for young Saudis as drone operators, environmental data analysts and aircraft maintainers.
  • The Kingdom owns the dataAll maps, counts and results stay under Saudi control and support SGI reporting.

03 / The fleet

Three aircraft. Each with a clear climate job.

Think of them as a team: one inspects up close, one surveys big areas and one carries heavy loads to places with no roads.

EGX-10

The close-up inspector

Light autonomous VTOL

  • Payload up to 10 kg
  • Flight time up to 2 h electric · ~4.5 h hybrid
  • Detail a few cm per pixel

Best climate jobsTree health, leak finding, steep mountain slopes, counting seedlings.

EGX-200

The long-range surveyor

Heavy autonomous VTOL

  • Payload up to 200 kg
  • Flight time up to 6 h
  • Range 400 km

Best climate jobsRegional mapping, cloud measurement, wildlife counts at night, dust-source surveys.

Converted helicopter

The heavy lifter

Existing helicopters, made unmanned

  • Lift class 1,000–3,000 kg (target)
  • Crew on board none
  • Built from suitable existing airframes

Best climate jobsDelivering seedlings, water tanks, solar pumps, fencing and weather stations to places with no roads.

The problem today

Riyadh is planting millions of young trees. In summer heat, a tree with a blocked drip line can die within weeks. Crews walking street by street cannot check every tree every week.

How the mission works

  1. 05:30 · Launch

    EGX-10 takes off at dawn. This is when heat-stressed trees show up most clearly on the thermal camera.

  2. 05:30–07:30 · Fly

    It flies a pre-set grid over the corridor, recording color, plant-health (multispectral) and thermal images.

  3. 08:00 · Analyse

    Software marks every tree as healthy, stressed or dead, each with its GPS position.

  4. 09:00 · Act

    Crews get a short list on their phones, for example "37 trees, 4 drip lines, these streets". They go straight to the problem.

  5. Repeat

    Weekly in summer and monthly in winter. Every flight adds to the tree-by-tree history.

Planning estimate: about 200–400 ha checked in each 2-hour EGX-10 flight. The pilot will confirm the exact figure.

What the Kingdom gets

  • Fewer trees lost and fewer trees bought again to replace them
  • Crews sent to the right street instead of blind patrols
  • A tree-by-tree record that proves survival to leadership at 6, 12 and 24 months
Already underway in the KingdomGreen Riyadh plans 7.5 million trees by 2030, irrigated with treated water.

How we prove it

  • Tree survival % compared with similar areas without patrols
  • Trees replaced per km of corridor
  • Crew hours per km checked

The problem today

Water is the Kingdom's most precious resource. Leaks in buried or drip lines and over-watered patches waste water for months before anyone sees them.

How the mission works

  1. Step 1 · Wide scan

    EGX-200 flies the whole irrigation network, up to 400 km in one flight, with a thermal camera. Wet ground shows up cooler than dry ground.

  2. Step 2 · Flag

    Software flags wet spots where there should be none (leaks) and dry spots where trees are thirsty.

  3. Step 3 · Close look

    EGX-10 returns to each flagged spot and confirms the problem at centimeter detail.

  4. Step 4 · Fix & confirm

    The field team repairs the line, and the next flight confirms the fix worked.

EGX-200 reference: up to 6 hours and 400 km per flight.

What the Kingdom gets

  • Leaks found in days, not months
  • Water sent where it is needed: to trees and crops, not into the sand
  • One clear number for decision-makers: liters of water per surviving tree
Already underway in the KingdomThe Kingdom created a National Center for Water Efficiency and Conservation, and is widening the use of treated water for irrigation.

How we prove it

  • Leaks found and fixed
  • Water saved (meter readings before and after)
  • Water used per surviving tree
Proposed partner
MEWA · National Center for Water Efficiency and Conservation · irrigation operators

The problem today

The Kingdom aims for 100 million mangroves by 2030. The coasts are tidal, muddy and often far from roads. Choosing the right spots and checking which seedlings survived is slow work.

How the mission works

  1. Before planting · Map

    EGX-200 maps the coast at low tide, showing mud, water channels and existing mangroves. This marks the best planting zones.

  2. Planting day · Deliver

    A converted helicopter carries seedling pallets from the nursery to the shore. No new roads or boats are needed.

  3. After planting · Count

    EGX-10 counts surviving seedlings plot by plot at 3, 6 and 12 months.

  4. Learn

    Zones with poor survival are compared with good ones, so the next season plants smarter.

All three aircraft work on this mission. It shows the full fleet working together.

What the Kingdom gets

  • Higher survival because seedlings go where the conditions are right
  • Faster planting on remote coasts
  • Proof of progress toward the 100M goal and future blue-carbon accounting
Already underway in the KingdomMillions of mangroves have already been planted along Jazan, Makkah, Tabuk, Madinah, Asir and the Eastern Province, and drones are already used to choose sites.

How we prove it

  • Seedling survival % per planting zone
  • Cost per surviving mangrove
  • Hectares of established mangrove

The problem today

NCM flew 415 seeding flights in 2023 with manned aircraft. To prove and improve the results, scientists need much more data from around the clouds, before and after seeding, than manned research flights can collect.

How the mission works

  1. Morning · Choose

    NCM forecasters choose the target clouds for the day.

  2. Before seeding · Measure

    EGX-200 flies up to 6 hours, measuring humidity, temperature, droplets and particles near the cloud.

  3. Seeding · Compare

    The manned seeding aircraft does its run while EGX-200 keeps measuring the same cloud afterwards.

  4. Same day · Share

    Data goes straight to NCM scientists, building a large evidence base season after season.

  5. Later stage · Test

    If NCM sees value, test an unmanned seeding payload together. This depends on the science and on approvals.

Flying altitude, icing and weather limits will be confirmed with NCM before any cloud flight.

What the Kingdom gets

  • More measurement hours at lower cost and with no crew risk
  • Stronger evidence of how much extra rain seeding produces
  • Saudi-built aircraft serving national weather science
Already underway in the KingdomThe program has run since the 2000s, flew 1,300+ hours in 2023, and has been training Saudi pilots.

How we prove it

  • Research flight hours added per season
  • Number of clouds measured before and after seeding
  • Datasets accepted by NCM scientists
Proposed partner

The problem today

Big dust storms often start from specific patches of bare, broken ground. Fix those patches and less dust reaches cities, highways, airports and solar farms. The hard part is finding them across huge areas.

How the mission works

  1. After a dust event · Trace

    EGX-200 flies along the storm's path back to the likely source areas.

  2. Map

    It maps bare soil, broken crust, vehicle tracks and dying plants, and ranks the hot spots.

  3. Check

    EGX-10 checks the top sites up close and records ground measurements.

  4. Fix

    A converted helicopter brings fencing, mulch, seed and plants to sites with no road.

  5. Each season · Re-fly

    The same areas are flown again to see if the ground is holding.

To be clear: aircraft do not stop sandstorms. They help find and fix the ground that storms start from.

What the Kingdom gets

  • A ranked list of dust hot spots instead of guessing
  • Money spent on the patches that matter most
  • Over time, less dust risk for cities, roads, airports and solar plants
Already underway in the KingdomThe Kingdom hosts a regional center for sand and dust storm warnings, one of only four in the world.

How we prove it

  • Hectares stabilized
  • Change in plant cover at treated sites
  • Dust readings at the nearest monitoring stations
Proposed partner
NCM Regional Sand & Dust Storm Center · NCVC

EGX-200, EGX-10, Converted helicopter

The problem today

The ancient juniper forests of the southwest are declining because of heat, drought and overgrazing. The slopes are steep, and rangers cannot reach or check every tree.

How the mission works

  1. Fly the slopes

    EGX-10 follows the mountainside, keeping a steady distance from the trees.

  2. Score each tree

    Every juniper gets a health score: green, stressed or dying.

  3. Spot the threats

    Maps show broken fences and grazing damage inside protected zones.

  4. Summer · Fire watch

    The same flights watch for smoke and early fires in the dry season.

EGX-10 performance at 3,000 m altitude will be confirmed during the pilot.

What the Kingdom gets

  • A tree-by-tree map of a national natural treasure
  • Rangers sent to the right slope at the right time
  • Proof that new plantings and fenced zones are working
Already underway in the KingdomSoudah Development has planted about 165,000 native trees, and the park is fencing regeneration zones.

How we prove it

  • Junipers mapped and scored
  • Dieback rate, year on year
  • Sapling survival inside fenced zones

The problem today

Oryx, gazelles and birds of prey are being returned to the wild. The reserves are huge, and counting animals from the ground is slow and disturbs them.

How the mission works

  1. 21:00 · Launch

    EGX-200 takes off after dark with a thermal camera. Animals show up as warm points.

  2. Night · Fly quietly

    It flies 4–6 hours of straight survey lines, high enough not to disturb the herds.

  3. Count

    Software counts and maps animals, grouping them by size and species.

  4. Morning · Report

    Rangers get herd locations and numbers, plus any unusual vehicles or illegal grazing.

EGX-200 reference: up to 6 hours of flight.

What the Kingdom gets

  • Accurate counts without stressing the animals
  • Quick checks on newly released animals
  • Early warning of poaching or illegal grazing
Already underway in the KingdomIn 2025, NCW released Arabian oryx, sand gazelles and birds of prey into the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve.

How we prove it

  • Area surveyed per night
  • Count accuracy checked against ground counts
  • Incidents found and passed to rangers
Proposed partner
National Center for Wildlife · royal reserve development authorities

The problem today

Many climate sites have no roads. Building a track just to install one weather station or one solar pump costs time and damages the land it is meant to protect.

How the mission works

  1. Load

    At base, the team loads a water tank, solar pump, weather station or fencing.

  2. Fly

    The converted helicopter flies autonomously to the site and lowers the cargo on a sling.

  3. Return

    It flies back to base. There is no pilot to expose to heat, dust or mountain winds.

  4. Check

    EGX-10 inspects the installation from the air and confirms it is working.

The 1,000–3,000 kg class is the target for selected conversions. Each airframe will be validated.

What the Kingdom gets

  • No new roads cut through fragile land
  • No pilot risk in extreme heat, dust and mountains
  • One aircraft serving many remote sites across the Kingdom
Already underway in the KingdomThe Kingdom is building monitoring networks, rainwater dams and restoration sites in remote areas.

How we prove it

  • Deliveries per month
  • Cost compared with trucks or manned helicopters
  • Road-building avoided (km)

    07 / Why autonomous aircraft

    Not a replacement. The missing link between satellites and ground teams.

    Satellites see wide but not close. Ground crews see close but cover little ground. Manned aircraft cost a lot and put crews at risk. Our fleet covers the gap between all three.

    SatelliteGround crewsManned helicopterEMYRGEN fleet
    How much detailAbout 10 m per pixel (free public data). You see a field, not a tree.Very close, one tree at a timeGoodA few cm per pixel. Every single tree and drip line.
    How fastEvery few days, if the sky is clearSlow, a few km per daySame day, if a crew and aircraft are freeOn demand. A report by the same morning.
    Dust & cloudBlockedNot affectedFlies belowFlies below, within weather limits
    Roadless & steep landSees it, can't actHard or unsafeYesYes, and it can carry cargo there too
    Risk to peopleNoneHeat, terrainCrew at riskNo crew on board
    Built & run byMostly foreign operatorsSaudi teamsMostly imported aircraftBuilt, maintained and flown in Saudi Arabia

    09 / How we prove success

    Judge us by results on the ground, not by flight hours.

    Each pilot starts by measuring a baseline. Then results are compared with similar areas that had no flights. Saudi agencies can check every number.

    Trees that survive

    Survival rate at 6, 12 and 24 months, compared with similar sites without patrols.

    Water per surviving tree

    Liters used per living tree, and leaks found and fixed.

    Speed of response

    Hours from a problem being spotted to a crew being sent.

    Cost per result

    Cost per surviving tree, mangrove or stabilized hectare, not cost per flight.

    Science accepted

    Cloud and dust data that NCM scientists accept and use.

    Saudi people trained

    Saudi operators, analysts and maintainers certified each year.

    10 / From pilot to national scale

    Start small. Prove it. Then scale.

    The climate program follows the same 36-month timeline as Part I, so the first missions fly while the Saudi campus is being built.

    Months 0–3Choose and prepare

    Agree three pilot missions with Saudi partners, then sort out permits, data rules and baselines.

    • Recommended: M01 Riyadh, M02 Al-Ahsa, M03 Jazan
    Months 4–12Fly the pilots

    EGX-10 and EGX-200 fly regular missions. First survival and water results come at month 6, with a full review at month 12.

    Year 2Add science & heavy lift

    Cloud measurement with NCM, dust-source mapping and wildlife counts. First flights of the converted helicopter for remote logistics.

    Year 3+National scale

    Saudi-built aircraft from the campus and Saudi operators in the control room. All eight missions running across the Kingdom.

    11 / The first step

    Start with three pilot missions in twelve months.

    Riyadh trees, Al-Ahsa water and Jazan mangroves. Three missions with visible, measurable results within one year, run on the same platform as the national program.

    1. Name a climate counterpart

      A lead from MEWA / NCVC to work with EMYRGEN, plus focal points at NCM and the city authorities.

    2. Pick three pilot sites

      Confirm sites, permits and the baseline measurements used to judge success.

    3. Form the joint working group

      One Saudi–EMYRGEN group covering Part I (industry) and Part II (climate), with milestones tied to results.
